report.source_text: A computed tomography (CT) scan with intravenous contrast of the abdomen, pelvis, and thorax demonstrated opacification of the hepatic vein indicative of thrombosis. A hepatic fluid collection measuring 9 cm transversely along with multiple cavitary lesions was also seen in the lung fields bilaterally, which were suggestive of hepatic abscess and septic pulmonary emboli, respectively (Figures 1, 2).

report.source_text: The patient had serial thoracenteses to drain fluid collections and placement of a CT-guided drain. The patient’s clinical status improved over the course of the admission, and he was discharged on intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for four weeks.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 36-year-old male with a history of complicated diverticulitis presented with fever, dyspnea, productive cough with dark brown sputum, and epigastric pain. Admission labs showed elevated WBC, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and D-dimer suggestive of infection and liver involvement. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed hepatic vein thrombosis, a 9 cm hepatic abscess, and bilateral septic pulmonary emboli. Blood cultures grew pan-susceptible Streptococcus anginosus, and echocardiogram was negative for vegetation. The patient underwent serial thoracenteses and CT-guided drainage, with clinical improvement and discharge on intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Elevated WBC, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and D-dimer on admission
CT showing hepatic vein thrombosis, hepatic abscess, and septic pulmonary emboli
Blood cultures grew pan-susceptible Streptococcus anginosus confirming infectious etiology
Negative transthoracic echocardiogram ruling out endocarditis as embolic source
Clinical improvement with drainage procedures and IV antibiotics and discharge
